# The Quiet Genius of Doors

Doors are so ordinary that we forget to wonder about them. But think about it: a door is one of humanity's most elegant inventions. It's a solid wall that we've made movable—a boundary that bends to human will. Before hinges and latches, people lived in structures with gaps to crawl through or nothing at all. Then someone, somewhere, thousands of years ago, looked at an opening and thought: *What if I could seal this and unseal it at will?*

And the word "door" itself carries weight. It sits at the root of so many of our greatest hopes—"opportunity" comes from the Latin *ob portare*, to carry toward. We say "when one door closes, another opens," as though life is just a hallway of thresholds. We speak of "showing someone the door," of "storming doors" and "back doors." The door is where private becomes public and the other way around. It's the architecture of transition.

There's something almost ceremonial about doors. The pause before knocking. The creak of wood. The moment when someone opens up and you catch a glimpse of their world—books on shelves, shoes by the entrance, a dog who wants to meet you. A door doesn't just separate rooms. It stages encounters.

Next time you walk through one, pause. Feel the hinge. Appreciate the hinge. Someone invented the hinge.
